chunks: Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Hamza al-Sha'rani al-Amari, from the descendants of Ammar ibn Yasir, informed us, saying: Abu Muhammad Ubayd Allah ibn Yahya ibn Abd al-Baqi al-Adni (in Adna) narrated to us, saying: Ali ibn al-Hasan al-Ma'ani narrated to us, saying: Abdullah ibn Yazid narrated to us, from Yahya ibn Uqba ibn Abi al-'Aizar, who said: Muhammad ibn Hajar narrated to us from Yazid ibn al-Asam, who said:

A man asked Umar ibn al-Khattab: 'O Commander of the Faithful, what is the interpretation of 'Subhan Allah'?' He replied: 'In this wall, there is a man who, when asked, informs, and when left silent, he begins (to speak).' The man entered, and it was Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him). So he asked: 'O Abu al-Hasan, what is the interpretation of 'Subhan Allah'?' He replied: 'It is the glorification of the majesty of Allah Almighty and the declaration of His transcendence above what any polytheist has said about Him. When a servant says it, every angel prays for him.'

key_terms.تَعْظِيمُ جَلَالِ اللَّهِ: Glorification of the majesty of Allah
key_terms.سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ: Glorified be Allah (a phrase of divine transcendence)
key_terms.مُشْرِكٍ: Polytheist (one who associates partners with God)

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning and spiritual benefit of saying 'Subhan Allah' according to Ali ibn Abi Talib?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Mani al-Akhbar* highlights the unique scholarly authority of Ali ibn Abi Talib, portraying him as the living repository of divine knowledge who could be awakened from slumber to provide precise exegesis. By defining 'Subhan Allah' as a declaration of Allah's transcendence above polytheistic attributes, the hadith connects the phrase to the concept of *Tanzih* (divine purity), while the promise of angelic prayers underscores its spiritual efficacy in Shia devotional practice.
